A clip on an instrument track holds **MIDI notes**, not sound. Each note is only: *which key*, *when*, *how long*, and *how hard*
(**velocity**). The instrument turns them into sound when you play. So you can change any note, the tempo, or the instrument
afterwards, and nothing is lost. That is the big difference from **audio**, a recording of sound, which you can cut and move but not
re-voice note by note.

The **piano roll** shows the notes: pitch up the side (a piano keyboard on its edge), time across, each note a bar whose length is its length.

## Writing notes

The Keys track below has the four chords of a C Am F G loop as whole notes, and an empty Bass clip is waiting.

1. Click the clip on the **Keys** track. Its notes show in the piano roll. Click a key on the left to hear it.
2. **Draw**: click an empty spot to write a note one grid step long. Drag the note up or down to change its pitch, drag its right end to make it longer.
3. **Velocity**: the bars under the notes. Drag them down for softer notes. Shift+click several notes to select them, then use the Velocity slider.
4. **Transpose**: select notes (or none, for all) and press +12 / −12 for an octave, +1 / −1 for a semitone.
5. Select the **Bass** clip and write a bass line: one note a bar, the chord's root (C, A, F, G), then try root on 1 and 3.

<div class="mdaw" data-id="daw-pianoroll" data-preset="keys" data-show="transport tracks editor record"></div>

## Recording and quantizing

Clicking notes in is precise but slow. Most people **record** from a keyboard and then fix the timing.

1. Select a track (click its name). Press **● Rec** (or R): one bar of clicks to count you in, then it records. Play with the computer keyboard
   (**A W S E D F T G Y H U J K**: the white and black keys from C; **Z / X** octave down / up) or a MIDI keyboard plugged in (Chrome or Edge).
   Space stops; the take becomes a new clip.
2. Your notes will be a little early or late: that's human. **Quantize** (Q) moves them onto the grid. Set **Grid** to the smallest note you played first.
3. **Quantize 50%** moves them only half way: tighter, still human. Producers often quantize less than fully for this reason.
4. **Undo** (Ctrl/Cmd+Z) whenever an edit goes wrong. Every DAW keeps a long undo history: use it freely.

Quantizing to the wrong grid is the commonest beginner mistake: triplets forced onto a 1/16 grid, or a swung part straightened.
Listen after you quantize.

## In other DAWs

<div class="daw-map">

| | BandLab | Ableton Live | Logic Pro |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open the piano roll | Double-click a MIDI region | Double-click a MIDI clip (the MIDI Note Editor at the bottom) | Double-click a region (or Window → Open Piano Roll, **Cmd+4**) |
| Draw a note | Click in the MIDI editor | Draw mode (**B**) | Pencil tool |
| Velocity | In the MIDI editor | Velocity lane under the notes | Velocity in the Piano Roll |
| Play from the computer keyboard | The instrument track's keyboard | Computer MIDI Keyboard (**M**) | Window → Show Musical Typing |
| Record | **R** (count-in in the metronome menu) | Arrangement Record button (●), or **F9** | **R** |
| Quantize | Select notes, right-click → Quantize, or **Q** | Select notes, **Cmd/Ctrl+U** | **Time Quantize** menu, with a **Strength** slider |

</div>
